name: MKREFFUNC(name, type)
prose: Test-local macro (defined in stdc_count_ones_test.c and expanded by the stdbit test kernel with the names and unsigned types unsigned char, unsigned short, unsigned int, unsigned long and unsigned long long) that generates a static reference function "static unsigned name(type value)" for stdc_count_ones. The generated function counts the set bits by looping while value is non-zero, adding value & 1 to a counter and shifting value right by one, and returns the counter, the number of 1 bits in value (0 for value 0). It has no side effects. The loop ends because the generated functions are instantiated for unsigned types only, where the right shift reaches 0.
note: stdc_count_ones_test.c:2-15 read in full; stdbit-test-kernel.c line 20 (MKREFFUNC(REF, TYPE)) and the five unsigned instantiations in stdbit-test-framework.c lines 30-60 seen. Reviewer round 15 (for negative signed values the shift would not terminate) does not apply: only unsigned types are instantiated. Tally 1 wrong. Fix instead of drop because the macro generates real functions.

name: MKREFFUNC(name, type)
prose: Test-local macro (defined in stdc_first_leading_one_test.c and expanded by the stdbit test kernel for unsigned char, short, int, long and long long) that generates a static reference function "static unsigned name(type value)" for stdc_first_leading_one. The generated function returns 0 when value is 0. Otherwise it builds a mask bit holding the most significant bit of the type by shifting a 1 left until the next shift (cast back to the type) would be 0, then moves the mask right one step at a time, counting from 1, until bit & value is non-zero, and returns that count: the 1-based position of the highest set bit counted from the most significant end. It has no side effects.
note: stdc_first_leading_one_test.c:2-21 read in full. Previously dropped as a macro; the macro generates real functions, so it is fixed under the macro head name.

name: MKREFFUNC(name, type)
prose: Test-local macro (defined in stdc_first_leading_zero_test.c and expanded by the stdbit test kernel for unsigned char, short, int, long and long long) that generates a static reference function "static unsigned name(type value)" for stdc_first_leading_zero. The generated function complements value (value = ~value, converted back to the type) and returns 0 if that is 0 (every bit of the original is one). Otherwise it builds a mask of the most significant bit of the type and moves it right, counting from 1, until it hits a set bit of the complemented value, returning the 1-based position of the highest zero bit of the original value counted from the most significant end. It has no side effects.
note: stdc_first_leading_zero_test.c:2-22 read in full. The "value = ~value" assignment is on the macro's parameter of the generated function, narrowing back to the type on assignment. Previously dropped as a macro.

name: MKREFFUNC(name, type)
prose: Test-local macro (defined in stdc_first_trailing_one_test.c and expanded by the stdbit test kernel for unsigned char, short, int, long and long long) that generates a static reference function "static unsigned name(type value)" for stdc_first_trailing_one. The generated function returns 0 when value is 0; otherwise it starts with a mask of 1 and position 1 and shifts the mask left, increasing the position, until bit & value is non-zero, and returns that position: one plus the index of the least significant set bit. It has no side effects.

name: MKREFFUNC(name, type)
prose: Test-local macro (defined in stdc_leading_ones_test.c and expanded by the stdbit test kernel for unsigned char, short, int, long and long long) that generates a static reference function "static unsigned name(type value)" for stdc_leading_ones. The generated function builds a mask of the most significant bit of the type (shifting a 1 left until the next shift cast back to the type would be 0), then counts, starting from 0, while the mask is non-zero and mask & value is non-zero, moving the mask right each time, and returns the count: the number of consecutive one bits from the most significant end, up to the width of the type. It has no side effects.

name: do_values_test
prose: Test helper taking a writable byte array buf with writable bytes at buf[-1] and buf[len] (so buf must have one byte of slack on each side), the length len, an index i and a character value c; it returns nothing and the caller keeps ownership of buf. It stores c (converted to unsigned char) in the two sentinel bytes buf[-1] and buf[len], fills buf[0..len-1] with c + 1 (converted to unsigned char by memset, so it wraps for c = 255), and if i < len stores c at buf[i] and records a check failure (ATF_CHECK_EQ, which does not abort) unless memrchr_fn(buf, c, len) returns buf + i; if i >= len it records a check failure unless the result is NULL. Nothing is restored afterwards: the sentinels and fill remain in buf.
note: memrchr_test.c:73-85 read in full (memrchr_fn is a function pointer set elsewhere, not read). Reviewers: round 1 (sentinels hold c and buf[i] is left as c; nothing restored) right; round 2 (the fill is c + 1 truncated to unsigned char, so c = 255 gives 0) right, memset(buf, c + 1, len) at 78; round 15 (ATF_CHECK_EQ is non-fatal, so the old claim of aborting is wrong) right. Tally 3 right.

name: ATF_TC_BODY(badparent, tc)
prose: Generated function badparent_body(tc), the body of an ATF test of cpuset parent assignment; it returns nothing. skip_ltncpu(2, &mask) obtains the CPU mask (the test is skipped on a machine with fewer than two CPUs). It records the calling thread's current cpuset id (origsetid), creates a new cpuset with cpuset(&setid) (which becomes the thread's set), clears the first CPU of the mask, sets the thread's affinity to that reduced mask, then sets the process's cpuset id back to origsetid with cpuset_setid and reads the thread's cpuset id again as finalsetid. Each of these calls must return 0 (ATF_REQUIRE_EQ), and finally finalsetid must equal origsetid; any failure fails the test.
note: slice cut the head and its visible lines belonged to the preceding test (jail_nproc, lines 690-775, which the previous prose described); the real function is the ATF_TC_BODY(badparent, tc) at cpuset_test.c:783-809, read in full. skip_ltncpu was not read. The previous prose described the wrong test.

name: token
prose: Reads the next token from the static stream cfile (a netrc-style file) into the static 100-byte buffer tokval and returns a code. It returns 0 immediately, without touching tokval, if feof(cfile) or ferror(cfile) is true on entry. It skips newline, tab, space and comma characters; reaching end of file while skipping returns 0 (tokval untouched). If the first character is '"' it reads up to the closing quote or end of file, otherwise it takes that character and reads up to the next newline, tab, space, comma or end of file; in both forms a backslash makes the following character be taken literally (in the unquoted form not for the first character, which is stored as is), and end of file after a started token still gives a token. It NUL-terminates tokval with no check against its 100-byte size, so a longer token overruns the buffer. If the token is empty (an empty quoted string) it returns 0 with tokval[0] == 0. Otherwise it compares tokval against the table (default 1 DEFAULT, login 2 LOGIN, password and passwd 3 PASSWD, account 4 ACCOUNT, machine 11 MACH, macdef 5 MACDEF) and returns the matching code, or ID (10) for any other token.
note: rexec.c:93-129, the token table at 71-82 and the buffer declaration at 70 read. Reviewers: round 2 (EOF while reading a token still returns the token, not 0) right, 115-123; round 15 (a leading backslash of an unquoted token is not treated as an escape) right, 114; original (contract omissions) moot. Tally 2 right. The old prose also claimed a precondition on token length; the code has no bound check, so overrun is possible for tokens of 100 characters or more.

name: parse_dialogrc
prose: Loads the dialog(1) configuration file into the library's globals; it takes no arguments. If the environment variable named by ENV_DIALOGRC is set and non-empty, the path is that value (truncated to PATH_MAX). Otherwise, if ENV_HOME is set, the path is its value, followed (only when the value is non-empty, shorter than PATH_MAX - 1 and does not end in '/') by a '/', and then by DIALOGRC if room remains; an empty HOME gives a path that is just DIALOGRC with no leading slash. If neither variable provides a path it sets errno to ENOENT and returns -1 immediately, without changing use_shadow, use_colors or gauge_color. Otherwise it calls parse_config(dialogrc_config, path, NULL, FIGPAR_BREAK_ON_EQUALS) and keeps its result res; whether or not that call succeeded, it then sets use_shadow and use_colors from the boolean values and copies the gauge_color string value (into the STR_BUFSIZE buffer with snprintf) from dialogrc_config_option's entries, which hold defaults for options not found in the file, and returns res (the result of parse_config).
note: dialogrc.c:284-325 read in full (slice began mid-function). parse_config and dialogrc_config_option not read. Reviewers: round 1 (globals not refreshed when HOME is unset) right, 308-311; round 15 (no slash when HOME is empty, len == 0) right, 299. Tally 2 right. The meaning of res (0 or -1) was not checked in parse_config.

name: DevPathFromTextDns
prose: Builds a DNS messaging device-path node from TextDeviceNode, a NUL-terminated CHAR16 string of comma-separated server addresses, and returns it, or returns NULL. It first duplicates the string (NULL if that fails) and counts the comma-separated tokens by walking the copy with GetNextParamStr, then frees the copy; if the count is 0 it returns NULL. It allocates a node of length sizeof(EFI_DEVICE_PATH_PROTOCOL) + sizeof(UINT8) + count * sizeof(EFI_IP_ADDRESS) with CreateDeviceNode (NULL if that fails). It scans the original TextDeviceNode for the first '.' or ':' to set IsIPv6 to 0x00 or 0x01 (left as CreateDeviceNode set it when neither character appears). It then calls GetNextParamStr on TextDeviceNode itself for each address, which overwrites each separating comma in the caller's string with a NUL and advances the local pointer, and parses each token with StrToIpv4Address (IPv4 case) or StrToIpv6Address (IPv6 case) into the matching DnsServerIp entry; the parse return values are ignored. It returns the new node. The caller's string is therefore modified (commas become NUL) in the final loop, not read-only.
note: slice cut the head; real function DevPathFromTextDns at efivar-dp-parse.c:3045-3125, read in full; GetNextParamStr/SplitStr read (173-213, 225-233: SplitStr writes *Str = '\0' over the separator at 202). Reviewer round 15 (GetNextParamStr writes NUL over commas, so the caller's string is modified; the old prose said never modified) right. Tally 1 right.

name: fetch_socks5_init
prose: Performs the SOCKS5 handshake on the open connection conn to ask the proxy to connect to host:port, returning 1 on success and 0 on failure. It logs the request, sends a 3-byte greeting (SOCKS_VERSION_5, SOCKS_CONNECTION, SOCKS_RSV) with fetch_write (failure code SOCKS5_ERR_SELECTION unless exactly 3 bytes were written), reads 2 bytes with fetch_read (SOCKS5_ERR_READ_METHOD unless exactly 2 were read), requires the first byte to be SOCKS_VERSION_5 (SOCKS5_ERR_VER5_ONLY), then fails with SOCKS5_ERR_NOMETHODS if the second byte is SOCKS_NOMETHODS and with SOCKS5_ERR_NOTIMPLEMENTED if it is anything other than SOCKS5_NOTIMPLEMENTED. It then builds the request in the local buffer (version, connect command, reserved byte, address type domain name, the host length byte, the host bytes, and the port in network byte order); a host longer than FQDN_SIZE gives SOCKS5_ERR_HOSTNAME_SIZE (this is an error path, not a precondition), and a write that does not send the whole request gives SOCKS5_ERR_REQUEST. It reads the reply into the BUFF_SIZE buffer and only treats a return of 0 as a failure (SOCKS5_ERR_REPLY); a -1 from fetch_read is not caught, and the buffer's contents are then examined as they are. The first reply byte must be SOCKS_VERSION_5 (otherwise SOCKS5_ERR_NON_VER5_RESP) and the second selects the result: SOCKS_SUCCESS continues, and the other documented status codes and any unknown status each map to a SOCKS5_ERR_* code. Every failure path calls socks5_seterr with the code and returns 0; the success path returns ret, which is 1. The verbose parameter is not used in the function body.
note: common.c:412-528 read in full; fetch_read/fetch_write/socks5_seterr not read. Reviewers: original (the reply check only catches 0, not -1) right, 480-483; round 15 (the hostname-too-long path means the precondition cannot require length <= FQDN_SIZE) right, 462-465. Tally 2 right. The `verbose` parameter appears unused; fetch_verbose is called without it (423).

name: hbsdctrl_feature_prohibit_ptrace_capsicum_apply
prose: Stores the requested state of the "prohibit ptrace on Capsicum processes" feature in two extended attributes on the file descriptor *arg1, and returns RES_SUCCESS or RES_FAIL. arg1 points to an int descriptor and arg2 to the feature state; the function returns RES_FAIL immediately if either is NULL, if the descriptor is negative, or if the state's value is not valid. Otherwise it writes a 2-byte buffer whose first byte is '1' if the value is HBSDCTRL_STATE_ENABLED and '0' otherwise to the ATTRNAME_ENABLED attribute in ctx->hc_namespace; if extattr_set_fd does not return 2 it returns RES_FAIL and does not write the second attribute. It then writes the buffer with first byte '1' if the value is HBSDCTRL_STATE_DISABLED and '0' otherwise to ATTRNAME_DISABLED; a result other than 2 returns RES_FAIL after the first attribute was already written. Only the first byte of the buffer is ever set (the second byte is left uninitialised and is written too). On success it sets HBSDCTRL_FEATURE_STATE_FLAG_PERSISTED on the state and returns RES_SUCCESS; the flag is not set on any failure path.
note: prohibit_ptrace_capsicum.c:140-179 read in full. Reviewers: original (contract omits the PERSISTED flag and the writes) moot, contract cleared; round 15 (the disabled attribute is skipped when the first write fails; the old prose said it may be partly written) right, 165-168. The buf[1] byte is never initialised (145, 164, 170).

name: hbsdctrl_feature_prohibit_ptrace_capsicum_get
prose: Reads the stored state of the "prohibit ptrace on Capsicum processes" feature from two extended attributes on the file descriptor *arg1 into the state *arg2, and returns RES_SUCCESS or RES_FAIL. It returns RES_FAIL at once if arg1 or arg2 is NULL (there is no check of the descriptor value). It first sets the state value to HBSDCTRL_STATE_SYSDEF. It queries the size of ATTRNAME_ENABLED; if the size is not positive it returns RES_SUCCESS when errno is ENOATTR (nothing stored, the value stays SYSDEF) and RES_FAIL otherwise. Having found the attribute it sets the PERSISTED flag, and returns RES_FAIL with the value INVALID if its size exceeds 2. It reads the attribute into a calloc'd buffer (RES_FAIL if calloc fails, leaving the value SYSDEF; value INVALID and RES_FAIL if the read fails) and takes enabled = (first byte == '1'). It then does the same for ATTRNAME_DISABLED, except that a size of zero or less, a size over 2, or a failed read all give value INVALID and RES_FAIL (a calloc failure gives RES_FAIL without changing the value), and takes disabled = (first byte == '1'). If both enabled and disabled are true the value becomes INVALID and it returns RES_FAIL; otherwise the value becomes ENABLED if enabled and DISABLED if not (also when neither flag was '1'), and it returns RES_SUCCESS. The buffers are freed on each path after allocation.
note: slice cut the tail; real function at prohibit_ptrace_capsicum.c:207-296 read in full, so fixed instead of dropped. Reviewer on the old drop (the first extattr_get_fd failure leaves SYSDEF, not INVALID) right, 225-233; the PERSISTED flag is set only after the first size query succeeds (236).

name: _citrus_EUC_mbrtowc_priv
prose: Restartable conversion of one EUC multibyte character from *s (n bytes available) to a wide character, using the partial-character state psenc; it returns 0 or EILSEQ and reports the byte count or status through *nresult. If *s is NULL it re-initialises psenc with _citrus_EUC_init_state, sets *nresult to 0 and returns 0 without writing *pwc. Otherwise it remembers the previous psenc->chlen, and when no byte is buffered it takes the first byte from the input (if n is 0 it goes to the restart exit); a buffered chlen of 1 or 2 continues; any other chlen is an encoding error. The code set is taken from the first byte and the character length c from ei->count (c == 0 is an encoding error). It then appends bytes from the input until chlen reaches c; if the input runs out it takes the restart exit, which sets *nresult to (size_t)-2, stores the advanced pointer into *s and returns 0, leaving the partial bytes in psenc. When the character is complete it sets *s to the advanced pointer, assembles the wide character (skipping the leading SS2/SS3 byte for code sets 2 and 3), masks it with ei->mask and ei->bits[cs], clears psenc->chlen, writes *pwc when pwc is non-NULL, sets *nresult to the number of bytes consumed in this call for the character (c minus the previously buffered length), or to 0 when the wide character is zero, and returns 0. The encoding-error exit clears psenc->chlen, sets *nresult to (size_t)-1, returns EILSEQ and does not update *s.
note: citrus_euc.c:193-274 read in full; _citrus_EUC_cs and _citrus_EUC_init_state not read. Reviewer on s == NULL path (resets state, *nresult = 0, returns 0 without storing a wide character) right, 202-206; the old prose also contained it. The old prose did not say the restart exit advances *s while the encoding-error exit does not (272 vs 265-268).

name: _ISO2022_sgetwchar
prose: Reads one character from the n bytes at string in an ISO-2022 stream, updating the shift state in psenc, and returns either the decoded wchar_t or _ISO2022INVALID, setting *result (if result is non-NULL) to the position after what it consumed on most returns; ei is unused. It first loops over control sequences, consuming each and continuing: SI/SO set psenc->gl to 0 or 1; the single-shift bytes 0x8e/0x8f set both singlegl and singlegr; a complete escape sequence found in seqtable that designates a character set stores the set's type, final, intermediate and version bytes in psenc->g[i] (an unexpected table type returns _ISO2022INVALID without setting *result); ESC n/o set gl to 2 or 3, ESC ~ } | set gr, ESC N/O set singlegl. A non-ESC byte ends the loop; an unrecognised or incomplete escape sequence ends the loop too, except that a prefix of a known sequence that is the whole remaining input returns _ISO2022INVALID with *result = string (more input needed). With no input left (n < 1) it returns _ISO2022INVALID with *result = string. A control character (iscntl) is returned as is (masked to 0xff), as is any byte for which the selected set is -1; the set is gr (or singlegr) for bytes with the high bit and gl (or singlegl) otherwise. For multibyte sets it returns _ISO2022INVALID with *result = string if fewer than 2 (or 3, when the final byte says three-byte) bytes remain or when the bytes do not all have the same high bit; for single-byte sets if no byte remains. A byte (or byte pair) outside the 94 or 96 range is returned as is, one byte consumed. Otherwise it assembles the wide character from the set's final byte, intermediate byte and the character bytes (special cases for ASCII ('B' with no intermediate) and ISO-8859-1 ('A' with no intermediate)), consumes 1 to 3 bytes, and returns it. In every path that returns a decoded character (as is or assembled) singlegl and singlegr are reset to -1.
note: slice cut the head; real function _ISO2022_sgetwchar at citrus_iso2022.c:576-840, read in full; seqmatch, iscntl, isthree, is94/is96 and the seqtable not read. Reviewers: round 1 (_ISO2022INVALID returns for incomplete multibyte length checks and the default type switch which skips *result) right, 636 and 741-770; round 2 (the length check also fails when enough bytes remain but the high bits differ) right, 746-753. Tally 2 right.

name: ifconfig_{*name*}_display(enum {*name*} v)
prose: Function template (in a Lua-processed template, instantiated by sfp.lua once per SFP enum named sfp_<name> whose last value has a display string) that generates ifconfig_<name>_display(enum sfp_<name> v). The generated function looks up v in the enum's metadata table with find_metadata, which scans the table entries until one has value v or the NULL-symbol terminator, and returns NULL if no entry has that value. If an entry is found it returns that entry's display field, a pointer to a static string, or NULL if that entry has no display string (the field is left NULL by the designated initialisers). The returned string must not be freed.
note: libifconfig_sfp_tables.tpl.c:92-103 (template text) and find_metadata at 14-20 read; the template is only instantiated when the Lua variable disp is set after the table-building loop (the last item's display), which I read in the template text but did not run. Previously dropped; the template does generate a real function. Reviewer round 15 (can return NULL for an existing entry without a display string) right, 41-42 vs 97-100. Tally 1 right.

name: _kvm_open
prose: Common open routine for kvm_open and friends: initialises the caller-allocated kd, opens the memory and kernel files, and returns kd on success or NULL on failure (after kvm_close). It sets vmfd, pmfd and nlfd to -1 and vmst, procbase, argspc and argv to NULL; it does not initialise the other fields (arch, rawdump, writable, resolve_symbol and the like), which must already be zero or set by the caller. If uf is NULL it uses getbootfile(); an exec file name of MAXPATHLEN or more characters fails with an error. A flag with bits other than O_RDWR fails with "bad flags arg". The memory file mf defaults to _PATH_MEM; it is opened (with flag | O_CLOEXEC) into pmfd, fstat'ed, and an empty regular file fails with EINVAL. If mf is a character device named _PATH_DEVNULL it opens /dev/null read-only into vmfd (the result is not checked, so vmfd may be -1) and returns kd immediately, and if it is _PATH_MEM it opens _PATH_KMEM into vmfd (failure goes to failed) and returns kd immediately; in both early returns nlfd stays -1 and the ELF header read, architecture probe, resolver check and ka_initvtop are skipped. Otherwise it opens uf into nlfd, calls _kvm_read_kernel_ehdr, sets rawdump and writable when mf starts with _PATH_FWMEM or _PATH_DEVVMM, probes the registered kvm_arch entries with ka_probe to set kd->arch (failure: "unsupported architecture"), fails with "non-native kernel requires a symbol resolver" for a non-native architecture without kd->resolve_symbol, calls ka_initvtop (failure goes to failed) and returns kd. At failed it copies the error buffer to errout (up to _POSIX2_LINE_MAX) when errout is non-NULL, calls kvm_close(kd) and returns NULL.
note: kvm.c:114-223 read in full (comments partly skipped); the callees (_kvm_read_kernel_ehdr, ka_probe, kvm_close) not read. Reviewers: round 1 (early /dev/null and /dev/mem returns skip the probe and ka_initvtop) right, 160-170; round 2 (vmfd open for /dev/null may fail yet kd is returned) right, 161-162; round 15 (kd->arch, rawdump, writable, resolve_symbol are never initialised here, so the precondition that fields need not be initialised is wrong) right, 119-125 only initialise some. Tally 3 right.

name: memstat_malloc_zone_used
prose: Reports whether the malloc size class n is marked in the type's size mask: it returns 1 if memstat_get_sizemask(mtp) & (1 << n) is non-zero and 0 otherwise. memstat_get_sizemask returns the 64-bit field mt_sizemask of *mtp (which must be a valid struct memory_type). The shift is done on a plain int constant 1, so the expression is only well defined for n from 0 to 30 (n = 31 shifts into the sign bit, and n >= 32 is undefined), which means the upper 32 bits of the 64-bit mask cannot be tested correctly. It allocates, frees and locks nothing and modifies no state.
note: memstat_malloc.c:536-543 read in full, memstat_get_sizemask at memstat.c:243-248. Reviewer round 15 (n < 32 is insufficient; 1 << 31 is undefined for signed int) right; the old prose also wrongly described the mask as 32 bits wide, whereas mt_sizemask is uint64_t. Tally 1 right.

name: _pam_exec
prose: Runs the program argv[0] (with arguments argv, argc >= 1) for PAM service function func with the options in *options, collects its output, and returns a PAM error code. Returns PAM_SERVICE_ERR if argc < 1, if the child is killed by a signal, or if the wait status is neither a signal nor a normal exit; PAM_BUF_ERR if reallocarray of the environment list, asprintf or strdup fails; PAM_SYSTEM_ERR if a pipe, fcntl, open of /dev/null, authentication-token fetch, pdfork, poll, read, write (other than EAGAIN) or waitpid (other than EINTR) call fails; otherwise, after a normal exit, the child's raw exit status when return_prog_exit_status is set, or PAM_SUCCESS for exit status 0 and PAM_PERM_DENIED for any other status. It builds the child's environment from pam_getenvlist plus the PAM items, PAM_SM_FUNC and (with return_prog_exit_status) the PAM error-code names; when expose_authtok is set it fetches the authentication token (from the stored item with use_first_pass or in pam_sm_setcred, else with pam_get_authtok) and feeds it to the child through a non-blocking stdin pipe; stdout and stderr go either to pipes (capture_stdout, capture_stderr) whose output is read and passed to pam_prompt as info or error messages, or to /dev/null. It forks with pdfork; the child sets up its descriptors and calls execve, calling _exit(1) if any step fails. The parent closes the child-side pipe ends, polls the process descriptor and the pipes until the process descriptor reports an event, then waits for the child. The cleanup at out preserves errno, closes pd and every pipe descriptor that is still >= 0, frees the environment list and returns pam_err. The descriptors chin[0], chout[1] and cherr[1] are closed after the fork but not reset to -1, so the cleanup closes them a second time (and the cleanup tests cherr[0] but closes cherr[1], so cherr[1] is closed twice when capture_stderr is set and is not closed at all on a failure before the fork when capture_stderr is not set).
note: slice cut the head; real function _pam_exec at pam_exec.c:160-460, read in full. Reviewers: original (may leak cherr[1] on an error path; returns the child's raw exit status or PAM_SERVICE_ERR) right: cherr[1] is only closed through the cherr[0] test (454-455); round 15 (parent closes cherr[1] before poll; cleanup double-closes it) right, 342-343 and 454-455, though the double close applies also to chin[0] and chout[1] (338-341 vs 444-451). pam_getenvlist may return NULL and is dereferenced unchecked (200-201). Tally 2 right.

name: pam_sm_authenticate
prose: PAM authentication entry point for the Kerberos 5 module: it authenticates the PAM user against the KDC and, on success, stores the credentials in a new in-memory ccache whose name it registers with pam_set_data under "ccache"; it returns PAM_SUCCESS or a PAM error code. It returns pam_get_user's or pam_get_item's (PAM_RUSER) error code immediately if they fail. It then duplicates the service name (PAM_BUF_ERR on failure), initialises the Kerberos context (PAM_SERVICE_ERR on failure), calls verify_krb_v5_tgt_begin (a failure is PAM_SERVICE_ERR unless the allow_kdc_spoof option is set), registers the memory ccache type (an error other than KRB5_CC_TYPE_EXISTS is PAM_SERVICE_ERR), builds the principal (user, or ruser/user with the auth_as_self option; the asprintf and strdup results are not checked for NULL) and parses and unparses it (PAM_SERVICE_ERR on failure). It obtains the password with pam_get_authtok (returning its error code); unless no_user_check is set, a user name containing '@' is mapped to a local name with krb5_aname_to_localname (PAM_USER_UNKNOWN on failure) and stored with pam_set_item, and getpwnam must find the user (PAM_USER_UNKNOWN otherwise). It then allocates credential options (PAM_SERVICE_ERR on failure), sets the forwardable flag if requested, and calls krb5_get_init_creds_password (PAM_AUTH_ERR on failure). With the TGT it creates a unique memory ccache, initialises it and stores the credentials (PAM_SERVICE_ERR on failure), runs verify_krb_v5_tgt (PAM_AUTH_ERR if it returns -1, destroying the ccache), returns PAM_AUTH_ERR (destroying the ccache) if a "ccache" item already exists in the PAM handle, builds the name "type:name" with asprintf (PAM_BUF_ERR if NULL) and registers it with pam_set_data using cleanup_cache (PAM_SERVICE_ERR on failure, destroying the ccache); on success ownership of the name string passes to the PAM framework. The cleanup labels free the credential contents (only on paths after get_init_creds), the principals, the context, the verify state and the duplicated service name, and a non-success result logs a message.
note: slice cut the head; the real function pam_sm_authenticate is at pam_krb5.c:114-400, read in full; verify_krb_v5_tgt*, cleanup_cache and the krb5 calls not read. Reviewer round 15 (creds contents not freed on early returns such as krb5_get_init_creds_opt_alloc failure) is wrong: creds is only populated after line 285 and the early paths jump to cleanup2, which correctly skips krb5_free_cred_contents (371); the krb5_get_init_creds_password failure path (289-294) also uses cleanup2. A separate observation is that the fall-through from cleanup3 calls verify_krb_v5_tgt_cleanup(krbctx, ...) after krb5_free_context(krbctx) (380, 385). Tally 1 wrong.

name: pam_sm_authenticate
prose: PAM authentication entry point that authenticates the user with a TACACS+ server and returns a PAM error code. It reads the conf and template_user options, opens a TACACS+ handle with tac_open, reads the configuration with tac_config and creates a login authentication request (each failure logs, closes the handle where one was opened, and returns PAM_SERVICE_ERR). It then passes PAM_USER, PAM_TTY and PAM_RHOST to the server through do_item, which returns the error code of pam_get_item if that fails (in this case the handle is not closed by do_item or by this function, so it leaks) and, when the item is set and the corresponding tac_set_* call fails, closes the handle and returns PAM_SERVICE_ERR; a non-success value from do_item is returned immediately. In the loop it calls tac_send_authen (on -1 it closes the handle and returns PAM_AUTHINFO_UNAVAIL), sets the echo option from the reply flags, and handles the status: PASS closes the handle and returns PAM_SUCCESS, after first, when template_user is set and pam_get_item(PAM_USER) succeeds, replacing PAM_USER by template_user if getpwnam does not find the user (an error from pam_get_item is returned after the close); FAIL closes the handle and returns PAM_AUTH_ERR; GETUSER and GETPASS fetch the server message (NULL gives PAM_SERVICE_ERR without closing the handle), obtain the user or password through pam_get_user or pam_get_authtok (an error closes the handle and is returned) and send it with set_msg (a failure returns PAM_SERVICE_ERR without closing the handle); GETDATA prompts with pam_prompt (error closes the handle and is returned) and sends the answer (set_msg failure returns PAM_SERVICE_ERR without closing); ERROR, RESTART, FOLLOW and any other status log, close the handle and return PAM_AUTHINFO_UNAVAIL. The loop repeats for the statuses that continue.
note: slice cut the head; the real function is pam_tacplus.c:108-270 with do_item at 65-80, both read in full. Reviewers: original (tach leaks when do_item's pam_get_item fails; errors from pam_get_user/authtok/prompt are returned) right, 71-73 and 137-152; round 15 (omits PAM_SERVICE_ERR when do_item's tac_set_* call fails) right, 74-78. Tally 2 right. The old claim that the handle is closed on every non-success return is wrong (139, 145, 152, 209, 224, 229, 244).

name: pam_sm_chauthtok
prose: PAM password-change entry point for pam_unix: flags selects the preliminary check (PAM_PRELIM_CHECK, tested first) or the actual update (PAM_UPDATE_AUTHTOK); it returns a PAM code. The user is getlogin() when the auth_as_self option is set (the result is not checked for NULL) and otherwise comes from pam_get_user (its error is returned). If getpwnam does not find the user it returns PAM_AUTHTOK_RECOVERY_ERR. Preliminary round: for uid 0 and a user from the local files (or, with YP, from NIS when ypclnt_havepasswdd reports a password daemon; failures are PAM_BUF_ERR or PAM_SERVICE_ERR) it returns the result of setting PAM_OLDAUTHTOK to "" without checking any old password. Otherwise the old password is "" if the stored hash is empty and the nullok option is set, or comes from pam_get_authtok(PAM_OLDAUTHTOK) (its error is returned); it then returns PAM_PERM_DENIED if the old password is empty and nullok is not set, or if crypt(old, stored hash) differs from the stored hash (so an empty old password only passes when the stored hash is empty too, and the crypt result is not checked for NULL), and otherwise returns PAM_SUCCESS (the pam_get_authtok result). Update round: it gets the old password (error returned) and the new password with pam_get_authtok, repeating while the result is PAM_TRY_AGAIN (other errors returned); a non-root caller with an empty new password and no nullok gets PAM_PERM_DENIED; pw_dup failure gives PAM_BUF_ERR. It sets the crypt format from the login class, sets pw_change from the passwordtime capability, creates a salt and encrypts the new password; for a files-sourced user it runs pw_init, pw_lock, pw_tmp, pw_copy and pw_mkdb, returning PAM_SUCCESS only if all succeed and PAM_SERVICE_ERR otherwise (pw_fini always runs); with YP a NIS-sourced user is changed through ypclnt_passwd (PAM_BUF_ERR, PAM_SERVICE_ERR or PAM_SUCCESS), and any other source gives PAM_SERVICE_ERR. With any other flags it returns PAM_ABORT.
note: slice cut the head; real function pam_sm_chauthtok at pam_unix.c:279-461, read in full; helper functions not read. Reviewers: original (root PRELIM round returns PAM_SUCCESS from pam_set_item without verifying the old token) right, 312-315; round 15 (an empty old password with nullok still requires the crypt match) right, 358-363. Tally 2 right.

name: get_args
prose: Reads the argument or environment strings of a core-dump process, located through the ps_strings structure at psstrings, and returns a buffer of the strings each followed by a NUL, with *lenp set to the number of bytes stored; type must be PSC_TYPE_ARGV or PSC_TYPE_ENVV (asserted). If args is non-NULL it is the caller's buffer and *lenp must be at least 1 (the capacity is the smaller of ARG_MAX and *lenp); if args is NULL it allocates an ARG_MAX-byte buffer, which the caller must free. It returns NULL, leaving *lenp unchanged, if reading ps_strings fails, if the address or the string count of the selected array is 0, if the count exceeds ARG_MAX (after a warning), or if allocating the temporary pointer array fails. It then reads the pointer array (failure goes to the fail exit) and, if it must allocate the buffer, allocates it (failure goes to the fail exit). For each string pointer it stops at the end of the array or at a NULL pointer, and reads the string in chunks of up to ARGS_CHUNK_SZ bytes, leaving one byte of the capacity spare; the number of bytes asked for in each chunk is treated as valid data (the byte count returned by core_read_mem is only compared with -1, so a short read leaves unread bytes in the length scan), and the string ends at the first NUL within the chunk, which is replaced by a stored NUL. If the capacity is exhausted it stops without terminating the last string. At the normal exit it sets *lenp to the bytes stored and returns the buffer (the caller's or the allocated one). At the fail exit (a failed pointer-array read, a failed buffer allocation or a failed core_read_mem in the loop, which returns -1) it frees the allocated buffer, if any, sets *lenp to the bytes stored so far (0 for the first two) and returns NULL. The temporary pointer array is freed on both exits.
note: core.c:380-462 read in full (slice began in an earlier region); core_read_mem not read. Reviewers: round 1 (does not set *lenp on the early NULL returns) right, 393-413; round 2 (omits the argv-array read failure; the buffer may not be NUL-terminated on truncation) right, 416-417 and 440-442; round 15 (a short core_read_mem return is ignored, so unread bytes may be counted) right, 443-448. Tally 3 right.

name: check_and_init_rwlock
prose: Resolves the pthread_rwlock_t stored at *rwlock into the actual lock object and stores it in *rwlock_out, returning 0 or an error code. If *rwlock is THR_PSHARED_PTR or is at most THR_RWLOCK_DESTROYED (that is, the static initialiser NULL, the destroyed marker 1, or any other value up to it) it returns the result of init_rwlock(rwlock, rwlock_out); otherwise it stores *rwlock in *rwlock_out and returns 0. In the init_rwlock case the possible errors are EINVAL (process-shared lock whose off-page cannot be found, or a destroyed lock) and ENOMEM (allocation failure while initialising a statically initialised lock); *rwlock_out is only written on a return of 0.
note: thr_rwlock.c:63-70, 73-94, 97-117 and 143-157 read in full. Reviewer round 15 (EFAULT cannot come from static initialisation since init_static passes a NULL attribute) right: rwlock_init returns EFAULT only in its pshared branch (110-112), which a NULL attr never reaches (101-102). Tally 1 right.

name: init_rwlock
prose: Resolves *rwlock into the actual lock object, performing lazy static initialisation, stores it in *rwlock_out and returns 0, or returns an error and leaves *rwlock_out unchanged. If *rwlock is THR_PSHARED_PTR it looks up the process-shared off-page lock with __thr_pshared_offpage(rwlock, 0) and returns EINVAL if there is none. Otherwise, if *rwlock is at most THR_RWLOCK_DESTROYED: for the static initialiser (NULL) it calls init_static for the current thread, which takes the static-init lock and, if the lock is still uninitialised, allocates and zeroes a lock structure with rwlock_init (NULL attributes), returning ENOMEM if the allocation fails (EFAULT cannot occur on this path), and the error is returned; for THR_RWLOCK_DESTROYED it returns EINVAL; any other small value falls through unchanged; the lock used is then the re-read *rwlock. For any other value it is used as is. It then stores the lock in *rwlock_out and returns 0.
note: thr_rwlock.c:73-94 read in full, with init_static (143-157) and rwlock_init (97-117). Reviewer round 15 (EFAULT impossible from static init) right.

name: rwlock_rdlock_common
prose: Acquires a read lock on *rwlock for the calling thread, optionally waiting until the absolute time abstime (NULL means no timeout), and returns 0 or an error code. It first resolves the lock with check_and_init_rwlock and returns its error (EINVAL for a destroyed lock or an unmappable process-shared lock, ENOMEM when static initialisation fails). If the thread already holds read locks (curthread->rdlock_count non-zero) it requests URWLOCK_PREFER_READER so a recursive read lock cannot deadlock behind a waiting writer. It tries _thr_rwlock_tryrdlock; on success it increments rdlock_count and returns 0. Only if that fails does it check abstime and return EINVAL if tv_nsec is 1000000000 or more or negative. It then loops on __thr_rwlock_rdlock(lock, flags, abstime) in the kernel, retrying in user space with another trylock when the call returns EINTR (so EINTR is not returned); any other result ends the loop. On a return of 0 it increments rdlock_count; any other result (for example ETIMEDOUT or EAGAIN from __thr_rwlock_rdlock) is returned with rdlock_count unchanged.
note: thr_rwlock.c:169-227 read in full. Reviewer round 15 (EFAULT cannot come from static initialisation) right; the old prose listed it.

name: _Tthr_rwlock_rdlock
prose: Implements the read-lock operation without a timeout (the pthread_rwlock_rdlock entry): it calls _thr_check_init() and returns rwlock_rdlock_common(rwlock, NULL). It therefore returns 0 with the calling thread holding a read lock and its rdlock_count incremented, or the error from rwlock_rdlock_common: EINVAL (destroyed lock or unmappable process-shared lock), ENOMEM (static initialisation failed) or an error from the blocking read-lock call such as EAGAIN; no lock is taken on an error return. EFAULT cannot come from static initialisation.
note: thr_rwlock.c:230-234 read; delegates to rwlock_rdlock_common (169-227). Reviewer round 15 right as for the others.

name: _pthread_rwlock_timedrdlock
prose: Implements pthread_rwlock_timedrdlock: it calls _thr_check_init() and returns rwlock_rdlock_common(rwlock, abstime), the absolute-time variant of the read lock. It returns 0 with a read lock held and the thread's rdlock_count incremented, or an error with no lock taken: EINVAL (destroyed lock, unmappable process-shared lock, or an abstime whose tv_nsec is out of range, checked only when the immediate trylock failed), ENOMEM (static initialisation failed), or an error from the blocking call such as ETIMEDOUT or EAGAIN. EFAULT cannot come from static initialisation.
note: thr_rwlock.c:237-242 read; delegates to rwlock_rdlock_common (169-227).

name: _pthread_suspend_np
prose: Suspends the thread given by handle thread, waiting until it is suspended, and returns 0 or an error code. If thread is the calling thread it returns EDEADLK without touching it. Otherwise it takes a reference on the target with _thr_ref_add(curthread, thread, 0) and returns that call's error code if it fails (no reference taken, no signal sent). When the reference is obtained it locks the thread and calls suspend_common(curthread, thread, 1), then unlocks it, drops the reference with _thr_ref_delete and returns 0 (the result of suspend_common is not used). suspend_common loops while the target is not PS_DEAD and not yet marked THR_FLAGS_SUSPENDED: it sets THR_FLAGS_NEED_SUSPEND on the target and, if the target's tid is TID_TERMINATED, returns at once with the flag set and no signal; otherwise it records the thread's cycle counter, sends SIGCANCEL, drops the thread lock, waits on the cycle counter in _thr_umtx_wait_uint (waitok is 1), retakes the lock and re-tests. Hence on a return of 0 the target is either dead, marked suspended, or has THR_FLAGS_NEED_SUSPEND set while its tid is TID_TERMINATED, and no signal is sent in the dead, already-suspended and TID_TERMINATED cases.
note: slice cut the head; the real function is thr_suspend_np.c:49-71, with suspend_common at 160-184, both read in full. Reviewers: round 1 (success can leave only THR_FLAGS_NEED_SUSPEND set for a TID_TERMINATED target) right, 167-170; round 2 (it does not always signal the target) right, 165-170; round 15 (TID_TERMINATED sets THR_FLAGS_NEED_SUSPEND before returning, so the flag is set even though no signal is sent) right, 167-170. Tally 3 right.

name: pt_dbsuspend
prose: Suspends (suspend non-zero) or resumes (suspend zero) the debuggee thread described by th and returns a td_err_e code (P2T converts proc_service errors). It returns pt_validate's error if validation fails. For a thread mapped as a raw LWP (type PT_LWP) it returns P2T of ps_lstop or ps_lcontinue on that lwp and does nothing else. Otherwise it reads the thread's attribute flags, TCB address and the mailbox's tm_lwp from the target with ps_pread, returning P2T of the first failing read. Only when the lwp is non-zero: if attrflags has bit 0x200 set it returns 0 immediately (without touching the mailbox dflags); for a system-scope thread (PTHREAD_SCOPE_SYSTEM) it reads the KSE lock level (and the thread's lock level if the KSE's is not positive) and stops the lwp only when suspending and the lock level is not positive, or continues it when resuming (a failing read or stop/continue returns P2T of the error); for other threads it calls ps_linfo (TD_ERR on failure) and stops the lwp when suspending unless PL_FLAG_BOUND is set in the info, or continues it when resuming (errors returned as P2T). With lwp zero none of that is done. It then reads tm_dflags, sets TMDF_SUSPEND when suspending or clears it when resuming, writes it back and returns P2T of the ps_pwrite result.
note: libpthread_db.c:440-542 read in full; pt_validate and P2T not read. Reviewers: original (PT_LWP path and the signal-thread return skip the dflags update) right, 454-460 and 480-481; round 15 (the 0x200 early return is inside the lwp != 0 block) right, 478-481. Tally 2 right.

name: libusb20_dev_get_port_path
prose: Copies the USB port path of device pdev into the caller's buffer buf (bufsize bytes) and returns the number of bytes written, or LIBUSB20_ERROR_OVERFLOW if the buffer is too small. If pdev->port_level is 0 (a backend without a port path) it returns LIBUSB20_ERROR_OVERFLOW when bufsize < 2 (buf untouched); otherwise it stores the parent address in buf[0] and the parent port in buf[1] and returns 2. If port_level is greater than bufsize it returns LIBUSB20_ERROR_OVERFLOW without writing. Otherwise it copies port_level bytes of pdev->port_path into buf and returns port_level.
note: slice cut the head; real function libusb20.c:750-772, read in full. Reviewer round 15 (port_level == 0 returns 0 after a zero-byte copy, not overflow or 2) is wrong: the port_level == 0 branch at 753-762 returns overflow or 2 before the copy at 769. Tally 1 wrong.

name: libusb20_desc_foreach
prose: Safely walks a block of USB descriptors described by pdesc (start pointer ptr and length len): given the current descriptor psubdesc (or NULL to begin) it returns a pointer to the next descriptor, or NULL at the end or when the data is inconsistent. It returns NULL if pdesc is NULL. The candidate is the start of the block when psubdesc is NULL, otherwise psubdesc plus its first byte (its length), which is read before any range check. It returns NULL if the candidate lies outside [start, start + len), if the address of the descriptor after it (candidate plus its own first byte) lies outside [start, start + len] (it may equal the end), or if the candidate's first byte is below 3. Otherwise it returns the candidate. It writes nothing; apart from the first byte of psubdesc it reads only the first byte of the candidate, after the range test.
note: slice cut the head; real name libusb20_desc_foreach at libusb20_desc.c:251-286 (not libusb20_me_get_next), read in full. The old prose is accurate for this function; the second-next check and the minimum length check come after the candidate's range test and read the candidate's first byte (277, 282).

name: hid_get_item
prose: Returns the next HID item of parser state s in *h, skipping items that do not belong to the selected report, and returns the result of hid_get_item_raw. It loops: each iteration calls hid_get_item_raw(s, h) and leaves the loop as soon as that result r is zero or negative, or s->reportid is -1 (no report selected), or the item's h->report_ID equals s->reportid; otherwise it discards the item and reads the next one. It returns r. In hid_get_item_raw (213-513) the only return values are 1, when an item has been stored, and 0 at the end of data, for a NULL s, for an invalid end collection, or for an invalid push/pop; so hid_get_item returns 1 for a stored item that matches the selected report (or when no report is selected) and 0 otherwise. s->reportid is only dereferenced after r > 0, so a NULL s (for which the raw function returns 0) is not dereferenced here.
note: slice 256-514 cut the head and covers the tail of hid_get_item_raw (213-513); the real hid_get_item is parse.c:516-526, read in full, with the return statements of hid_get_item_raw listed (221, 252, 350, 363 return 1 or 0; 359, 406, 418, 512 return 0) but its body otherwise not read ("partly read"). Reviewers (rounds 15 and 17: the code shown is a raw parse loop that never calls hid_get_item_raw) are right about the slice shown but not about the function hid_get_item itself, which does call hid_get_item_raw and filter on report_ID (521-523). Tally 2 mixed.

name: vcpu_reset
prose: Sets the guest register and descriptor state of virtual CPU vcpu to the x86 power-on reset values using vm_set_register and vm_set_desc, in this order, and returns 0 if every call succeeded; at the first call that returns a non-zero error it stops and returns that error, leaving the earlier registers already written. The values are: RFLAGS 0x2, RIP 0xfff0, CR0 = CR0_NE (not the architectural reset value, as the code comment explains), CR2, CR3 and CR4 zero; CS with base 0xffff0000, limit 0xffff, access 0x0093 and selector 0xf000; SS, DS, ES, FS and GS with base 0, limit 0xffff, access 0x0093 and selector 0; EFER, RAX, RBX, RCX, RSI, RDI, RBP, RSP and R8 to R15 zero and RDX 0xf00; GDTR and IDTR with base 0, limit 0xffff and access 0; TR with base 0, limit 0, access 0x8b and selector 0; LDTR with base 0, limit 0xffff, access 0x82 and selector 0; DR6 0xffff0ff0, DR7 0x400 and the interrupt shadow 0.
note: slice cut the head; real function vcpu_reset at vmmapi_machdep.c:421-607, read in full (excerpt began at the GDTR/TR code, so the old prose lacked the first registers: RFLAGS, RIP, CR0, CR2-4, CS and the data segments). vm_set_register/vm_set_desc not read.
